review: Give us co-op and workshop and this is fucking game of the year for me, absolutely love it.

Teardown is one of those rare games that manage to deliver a large quantity of content with so much freedom for possibilities while offering insane levels of destruction. 

I've played it for a little while, having picked it up when it first released as early access on steam and its development has been amazing to watch. With entirely new campaigns and massive boosts to the games performance, modding capabilities, and base game throughout. 

[h2] Destruction[/h2]
Originally I was drawn to it after hoping for something to rekindle that feeling of Red Faction: Guerrilla and other destruction focused games, Teardown more than delivered on that front. Pretty much everything can be destroyed in many different ways, structures can even catch fire, fire which then spreads in a realistic fashion, burning buildings down to the ground or making them a burnt out husk. 

It really is a game where a building with a locked door can be resolved in many ways: Breaking through a nearby window, using your blowtorch to burn out the lock, or just driving a piece of heavy construction machinery through the wall. 


[h2] Story / plot [/h2]
In terms of story and plot, your character operates a small family run business that had previously been struggling to keep the lights on. Until one day you get an email to perform a somewhat "unauthorised demolition" from here things just grow larger, seeing you knocking down towers, stealing priceless art, causing petty vandalism against a wealthy car owner. Eventually you find yourself stealing military weapons, visiting tropical islands, uncovering dastardly plots, and you also get to fight killer robots! 

[h2] Modding [/h2] 

It's safe to say that from my perspective, the game has a wonderful and vibrant modding community, with plenty of active modding support provided by the devs, and a decent API to work with. Modders have made things ranging from advanced weapons to destroy structures, functional portal guns, AC 130 airstrikes, massive amounts of high quality vehicles from movies and real life, entire custom levels  and even campaigns that involve high quality detailing and interaction for players to enjoy.  There have even been mods made that completely change the nature of the game, such as turning it into a fire fighter sim, a hack and slash shooter game, even old school games. In effect the modding allows people to turn the engine to make whatever they can think of. 


[h2] The Devs [/h2] 
The devs simply have been amazing. Really friendly and active with the community on the games discord. Quite often you'll find the devs getting really engaged with whatever creations modders are coming up with, and having very good discussions with the community, clearly laying out plans and often delivering more than we could have hoped for in the community. This is one of those games that have been boosted by having such active and driven devs who genuinely care about the game. 


[h2] Conclusion / Should I buy / TL:DR [/h2]


Teardown is a fantastic game filled with plenty of content to keep you busy. It more than is worth its initial cost and the content keeps growing from there. 
Personally I've found it to be exactly the game I had wanted for a long time but just hadn't seen delivered anywhere near as well as it has been here. 10/10 would recommend again.

Purchased the game expecting to dawdle around in a sandbox for a bit now and then. Ended up tearing through much of the campaign after playing it for 7 straight hours in one sitting.

The physics are really brilliant. One thing I did was take a blowtorch to a refrigerator to tear the door off of it, which I then glued it to the top of a water-sensitive safe so that I could carry it through the rain without setting off its alarm. The game doesn't necessarily intend for you to do this, but the physics engine just happens to allow for it to work.

Planning routes is incredibly invigorating once you've started feeling it out. I don't know if this is the case for everyone or just me, but I made very good use of my spray paint tool to draw out my path as I went along. Other times it can be fun to forgo the bonus objectives, grab the shotgun, and just blast through walls as you frantically run through the level without scouting anything out (which is often much more of a challenge).

Oh, and the sandboxy elements still work. Nothing is stopping you from just blowing everything up just to watch the world burn (except for your limited ammo, but custom maps via mod support can and do fix that).

It's not often I recommend a game so quickly after playing it for the first time. This game is pretty good.
I love this game, I can clearly remember the day I first got it. I blew up a house, stole some paintings, knocked down a tower, then went home and played Teardown.

[h1]Another awesome game about blocks developed by a Swedish guy.[/h1]

Like, [i]too[/i] good. Everything is amazing, the graphics, the physics, the gameplay, the countless missions, the maps, the sandbox, the driving mechanics, the level creator, the tools-- everything.
I've followed this game since it first got teased almost two years ago, and it's done nothing but improve and wow me since. I remember when it was just a simple physics test, but over time, it bloomed into a full-blown game.
I stayed up all night waiting for the release of this game, and boy was it worth it.

However, don't be fooled by its seemingly simple blocky graphics, this game requires serious hardware to run well. Especially if you have an AMD card. You'll need a [i]very[/i] good one. Also a really good CPU.

This is one of the most innovative and addicting games I've ever played, and I'm so happy seeing how far it's come.

A lot of the reviews for this game boil down to "HAHA DESTRUCTION FUN AND GOOD THEREFORE RECOMMENDED" without really delving into what makes [i]Teardown[/i] fun,  while also ignoring the game's serious shortcomings that it currently has while in Early Access. 

To begin, [i]Teardown[/i] is a solid puzzle game with sandboxy destruction elements. Each mission you're dropped into an open sandbox and given an objective of some kind, usually "destroy/obtain a series of objects spaced around the map", with completing the first objective usually triggering a one minute alarm. When the alarm counts down to zero, you lose. This simple concept is enough to carry the gameplay of [i]Teardown[/i] pretty far, since each mission gives you a new twist on your objective. One mission you could be picking up keys, the next you could be tossing safes into water or crashing cars. Some missions even forgo the time trial idea and instead stick to simply allowing you to go nuts with the destructive capabilities of the game's voxel-based environments. You can really mess things up in this game, burning down walls, blasting apart doors and shattering windows to create optimal routes to complete each of the level's objectives under one minute. The sense of satisfaction and relief after successfully escaping is quite high and ultimately keeps the game entertaining throughout the first act.

However, [i]Teardown[/i] is currently replete with tons of issues that hamper the game's enjoyment. If you don't like the time trial gameplay, then tough shit, since that's the vast majority of missions on offer here. If you just wanna explore the Sandbox mode then tough shit too, since sandbox unlocks are tied to your campaign progress. The game also runs pretty poorly, but I assume that this will be fixed towards the end of development. The biggest issue that the game currently faces is issues with "balance", an odd thing for a sandbox game such as this. Simply put, certain tools and items are woefully weak compared to others, which makes using them a chore. Pipe bombs and the starting sledgehammer stick out the most, since the first is a hard to use and pathetically small explosive, and the second is your go-to demolishing tool that instantly becomes replaced by the much better shotgun, which can pierce through tougher substances. 

The nice thing about Early Access is that all of these issues can be fixed. As such, i'd like to offer some feedback and suggestions in equal measure.

* [b]Feedback[/b]
- BUFF THE SLEDGEHAMMER, PISTOL, AND PIPEBOMBS: As stated above, the sledgehammer sucks compared to the shotgun. Instead of nerfing the shotgun, I would suggest buffing the sledgehammer so that it can smash through brick. That way the shotgun can still blast through metal efficiently- perhaps lock a few of the doors around the map to incentivize using the shotgun to get around them. The pistol is another bad weapon since it's starting magazine size is a woefully small 6 rounds- it's easier to just use the blowtorch than use it. Maybe increase it's starting mag size so it can compete with the other metal-breaking solutions. Lastly, the pipebombs are incredibly unwieldy to use. I would keep their blast radius the same, but maybe add a throwing arc to assist with aiming them, since I can't count the times where I've tried to throw a pipebomb through a window only for it to land at my feet.
- INCREASE VEHICLE DURABILITY: This is the big one. Vehicles break so easily in this game that using them is more of a liability than a help. A simple tap against some surfaces can send huge chunks of vehicles scraping off, rendering powerful tools like excavators and bulldozers utterly useless. Increasing their durability so they can take more of a beating would make them easier to use. Trust me, I've seen bulldozers smash houses really easily and come out okay- their tractors are made of metal for a reason.
-  MAP IMPROVEMENTS: Another big one. The in-game map is not as useful as it could be. It only shows an overhead view of the level, and while the game clearly labels where each objective is, it's still confusing due to the numerous buildings you need to traverse. On stages like Hollowrock Island where multiple levels of elevation are a common element, this is a huge pain, since keeping track of where each objective is while planning out the stage is impossible without visiting each objective in-person. Being able to rotate the map like a 3D object would be helpful in regards to planning your route and could be a neat tool to admire the incredible destruction that's been caused by you. 

[b]Suggestions[/b]
- PLANNING SCREEN: I think turning the map into a makeshift planning screen could be very helpful for planning routes. Being able to draw on the map and have those drawings appear in the game world would be incredibly helpful, especially considering the game's pin-point accurate requirements for completing a 100% run of certain levels. You could draw paths to help you remember where to run, designate angles to stand and fire at, and give you reminders of what you wanted to do while initially planning the level. Adding something like this would make the game much more accessible to play and increase the level of satisfaction gained from successfully completing a mission. I know that the spraypaint already has some of this functionality, but I think the inventory is already very cluttered (something i'll talk about further down) so moving it's purpose to a designated planning screen would both lessen the inventory and make things easier for players. 
- NEW WEAPONS: I think some melee-weapon sidegrades could be in order. Maybe a fireaxe that swings faster but destroys a larger part of the environment when swung, or a sodering blade that's really slow but can slice through metal ala the welding flame from [i]Alien Isolation[/i]. I could also see a sniper-rifle with a bipod attachment for hitting far away targets, with the catch that the weapon can't be fired until it's placed down on the ground. You could also include some bomb alternatives, like a remote denoted variant with a smaller explosion radius, or an impact-detonated variant. If the game moves towards the "heist" angle even more, I could see tools like slingshots, ziplines, nightvision goggles and maybe even grappling hooks being added as well. 
- LOADOUT SWAPPING: I think the game's inventory is utterly massive as-is and adding anymore items would make managing them in the heat of the moment more difficult than it already is. Therefore, I think it would be best if you added a chest to the escape vehicle that allows you to store and take any of your currently obtained tools. This would also make running the route easier, since you don't need to scroll through your MASSIVE inventory while trying to run a gauntlet of your own design.
- ADJUSTABLE DIFFICULTY: It's fairly obvious that the difficulty is the game's most contentious aspect. I personally never found it too tough, but I agree that an "easy" difficulty that increases the time limit for each mission could be fun and helpful for people who aren't used to speedrunning games like this. As well, the one-minute time limit for every mission is kind of repetitive- maybe make some of the missions have laxer or harsher time requirements to encourage outside of the box thinking. I would also maybe convert leftover time from each mission into dollars earned, to more encourage optimisation in your routes.

I hope you take some of these ideas to heart since the game's current foundation is there, but these issues prevent it from being the best it can be. Oh well- that's what Early Access is for.

This game is wonderful.

From the satisfying explosions & realistic lighting and weather, to satisfyingly destructive fire and physics, Teardown is by far the most amazing game I have played in 2021. I may be a bit late to the party, but Teardown has the potential to hold up for the future. If this ever gets ported to next-gen hardware, it would be magnificent. Everything in the game is so amazingly satisfying. Teardown, I must say, is the ultimate stress reliever. There is something so magical about seeing semi-realistic destruction, with no real consequences. Don't even get me started on the infinite stream of modded weaponry, maps, and random features I didn't know I needed.

You like blocky games?
You like destroying stuff?
You like making shortcuts by blowing up buildings?
You like abusing saves to achieve the perfect game?

This is the game for you.

If you were the kind of person to go around burning minecraft villages in creative mode as a kid, this is the game for you.

One thing I do before buying a game on steam is read the bad reviews, I find that usually they point out a game's biggest flaw quite quickly and it helps me see if a game is going to annoy me to the point it isn't worth buying...

The bad reviews for this game all read the same way, "omg time limit bad, I want to blow things up" but now having played a few timed missions all I can say is, this game has me hooked.

It's such a simple idea, here's a bunch of stuff to steal in a cluttered level, once you touch one alarm box you have 60 seconds to grab the rest and leg it back to your sketchy van before the cops show up.. but the fun comes from planning, is there a box hooked up to a classic car?  Why not drive the flatbed truck that car is on as close as you can to the escape point?  Gotta get 3 cars in under 60 seconds?  Knock a hole in the side of a barn, build a series of plank paths along the rooftops, use a crane to carry the car to a boat... once you see how each level is designed and play around with the tools it becomes a hitman or classic rainbow six style planning game..except instead of studying guard movements for 40 mins you're knocking out windows and piling cars into rivers so you can find the quickest way into, and out of each mission.

You know those idiots who ram a car into a store, grab everything then drive off?  That is pretty much Teardown in a nutshell..and I love it.

10/10, would run a boat through a dockside cabin for the insurance money again.

When i was young, i always wanted a game when you can basically destroy everything, of course, there were some games where you can destroy things, like in GTA, or Just Cause, etc... But you can't destroy everything, except for Red Faction, for example. But since this game is getting 'old', i wondered if something more 'new' existed, and here it comes, Teardown.
And it became one of my favourite games.
The graphics, the gameplay, the destruction, this game has it at everything.

Of course, you will need a good PC to play it without seeing a PowerPoint instead of a game, and in terms of graphics, i saw that this game needs at least a GTX 1060 3GB VRAM. I have a GTX 960 2GB and it runs pretty well, even if i put the graphics in high, with 75% render scale, i'm not in full 60 fps obviously, but it's still very playable (~40-50 fps).

Now let's talk about the good points and the bad points. And of course, the game is in early access, so what i said can be outdated in the future.

Good points:
- Graphically beautiful
- Satisfying destruction
- Gameplay
- Easy to understand how to use the tools
- Price
- Updates
- Optimized loadings (unlike sometimes GTA V)
- Maps
- Workshop
- Pretty fun challenges if you're getting 'bored' of the sandbox and campaign modes

Bad points:
- The game becomes laggy if you destroy too much things (and it's normal since the PC has to manage thousands of voxels and the game is in early access)
- Large structures will not fall until the last voxel is disconnected (also normal otherwise the game would run at maximum 2 fps)

That's it, thanks for reading my review, if you have anything to say about it, you can write your thoughts in the comments below, stay safe and have a good day.

This is a tricky one to recommend!

On one hand, the first few hours of this game are absolute magic. This engine is badass, and the voxel destruction system works great and looks surprisingly good. There's tons of different vehicles and weapons and all sorts of neat stuff that let you destroy things in really creative and fun ways. The game also gives you infinite spray paint to graffiti anything you want anywhere which is worth a positive review in and of itself because I can ruin a man's livelihood and write "FART" on his lawn.

Where the game starts to get a little tricky for me is in its increasing focus on "heist" type missions. On paper this is SUPER cool, in fact when I played the first heist level I absolutely fell in love with the concept, but the game starts to rely VERY heavily on this "collect all objects and get out within 60 seconds" gameplay. Sometimes that'll be changed up in minor ways, i.e. "dump all cars in the water" or "blow up all generators", but the core gameplay loop is fundamentally the same. Where this gets tricky is that this gameplay loop isn't really conducive to a fun experience when combined with the voxel engine.

The voxel engine in Teardown is chaotic. Things can really spiral out of control quickly if you don't control for variables, entire buildings can be supported by one singular remaining voxel that you'll have to frantically look for in the heat of the moment in some levels, and cars control really badly and constantly get stuck on tiny curbs and rocks. To be honest I don't think this is a problem in itself! The problem comes when the game expects you to execute precision heists using this engine. It's like the gameplay and engine are fighting each other trying to be two different things.

The engine wants to be placed into a chaotic game, where you're blowing stuff up left and right and improvising solutions to your mistakes and so on. The game itself, though, is an exercise in patience and precision, where you will spend 30 minutes tinkering and tweaking and perfectly setting up your planned route to get all the objectives and then brute force attempts over and over until the engine cooperates with you. The game won't let you save and quit your setup halfway either, so EVERY time you launch this game and want to make progress you have to be committed to either finishing the 30+ minute long level in one go or accepting that all your time might be wasted if you have to or want to go do something else at any point. Long story short, the engine is intentionally messy and chaotic and built for destruction, but the game wants to be a precision puzzler speedrun game where the slightest hiccup means savescumming and trying again. An engine built for messy destruction and a gameplay loop that wants you to construct an optimal route and run it as perfectly as possible.

Nothing is quite as emblematic of this nagging issue as the fire system. The game provides you with loads of methods for starting fires, but the second a fire grows too big, the fire department is called and your heist fails. Beating a dead horse here, but in a game whose engine centers around creatively destroying your environment, putting out every little fire you start is not particularly fun.

The end result is that I never really feel my skill being tested in this game, or my intelligence. More so just my patience. How willing am I to spend time carefully setting up every tiny detail of this heist before I execute it? How many corners can I cut to save my own time that won't mess up my whole route? I rarely had to properly sit down and plan out a route, and my own skill at platforming and controlling the character was also seldom a factor. It was primarily just patience and prep time, which isn't exactly a fun or invigorating thing for a game like this. 

The story does some pretty dope stuff and the game is still overall a definite recommend. I also don't think I'm done playing it, as this is the kind of game I could spend hours on over time. But man, I can't help but think how much more this could be, which is actually exciting given that this engine has been made and the devs can now apply it to other ideas. I definitely recommend this game to anyone who seems interested by its engine and/or core concept, but I struggle to recall a game that gets less and less fun as you play as much as this game does. Easily worth it for the first hour alone though!

This game needs way more recognition. It's polished to a mirror sheen and paced like a champion. Somehow, despite being a voxel game, it looks incredibly realistic too. Like when people show off those crazy graphical mods for Minecraft, except this is just the base game.
And they're adding multiplayer soon??? This is the perfect game for anyone interested in feeling smart while recklessly blowing stuff up in first person. The sound effects are great too, and the music has kind of a chill, sneaky vibe. 
It's a dream of a game. Imagine being able to explore detailed, hand crafted 1-to-4-city-block-sized maps where you can literally level the whole place if you wanted to. And every voxel is individually physically simulated. It's crazy that we live in a world where games like this can exist. 
Wait until the sale ends and buy this one at full price.

The developers could have released just the sandbox and it would have more than justified the price tag, but they went absolutely beyond that with its campaign mode that elevated the novelty of the voxel physics into a wonderful mix of creative puzzle solving and action that scratched an itch I didn't even know I had.

The missions are widely varied and continually keep you on your feet with changing circumstances. They make wonderful use of the levels and force you to truly get to know every little detail about the area before you can even commit to anything. Tools are introduced slowly to allow full understanding of their potential, and the freedom to upgrade them to how you like really allows you to play to your exact preference.

There was obviously a lot of love that went into the level design. The tiny, unique details that went into every building and room really stands apart from obvious cut/pastes of assets that have become the lazy standard of AAA games. Fun little things like a working elevator in Gordon's mansion, a working racing track with time trails,  and other interactables prove this engine has some truly impressive capabilities. 

On top of all this, the game is clearly coded very well. My aging PC has no right to tolerate the sheer number of voxels flying around from a dam explosion, but somehow does alright. And the butter-smooth transition from map mode and back is incredible!

Honestly if this game had a AAA budget for voice acting and story, it would easily rival Valves Portal or even Half Life series. I am truly excited about the sheer potential of this engine and its developers. Well done guys!

Teardown is an absolutely fantastic PUZZLE, HEIST game, which involves patience, planning, and speed-running objectives. I stress this because most of the negative reviews come from a mismatched expectation that this game would involve vast amounts of destruction and/or combat. Teardown is simply not that. The most common mission type in the campaign involves grabbing an X number of objectives within 60 seconds and then getting back to your escape vehicle. This means that in most missions, you will be spending 10-20 minutes planning and "tearing-down" obstacles prior to triggering the 60 second 'heist', where you grab everything and get out. If a developer does end up reading this...I really think this game would benefit from a demo of ~5 missions. This would give players a chance to see if they like it, but also allow them to see if they have the hardware to run the game properly.

-- What I liked --
[list]
[*] The game is well worth the price with a lengthy campaign and high replayability. I expect the average person would take 15-30 hrs to complete the base 40 mission campaign, depending on how meticulous they plan and how many optional objectives they go for.
[*] Mission pacing is good, with some unique mission types sprinkled amongst the common '60 second heist' type missions. The objectives are challenging, but you can use mods or change some settings (like the timer) to make it easier to beat. Achievements are still obtainable with mods.
[*] Excellent level and voxel designs, especially when combined with the weather types. I loved every map, super detailed, highly immersive with lots of places and rooms to explore.
[*] Free mini expansion
[*] Mod support with an existing selection of great mods! (Love the AC130 mod, but it kills my fps!)
[/list]

-- What could be better --

[list]
[*] Campaign could do with more destruction missions. However I can see why Developers avoided this as the game does have understandable performance issues due to physics and voxel effects etc... Even with a 3080, once you get a few fires going with some big explosions, frames start dropping fast.
[*] Physics and weight does not apply properly to 'structures' or 'buildings'. This means that you could blow out supporting parts of a building, but it will remain floating in the sky as long as 1 voxel is still connected somewhere. (which I guess could also explain why there aren't a lot of demolition missions)
[*] No keybind for 'quicksave'....this one is kinda odd, considering you use this button so often. Barebones graphics and game settings overall.
[*] Game could do with a demo to manage expectations.
[/list]
If you have already been banned on every minecraft server for griefing and can't afford any more vandalizing in real life this game is for you.

I find that most of the negative reviews of this game focus on the campaign mode for the game.
I had originally bought Teardown in late 2020,  interested in it for its physics/voxel based destruction, and was similarly disillusioned and overwhelmed by the campaign mode. I refunded it that same day. I didn't care about the campaign, I just wanted to destroy stuff.

Three years later I re-purchased Teardown, still with the intention of completely ignoring the campaign. I played tons of sandbox + workshop mods and it was a very fun and satisfying time waster. The game has a very active modding community with many high-effort mods. The workshop content is essentially endless.

I eventually decided to try the campaign and found that it wasn't as bad as most people think.
Many of the missions are indeed timed missions, but the fun is mainly in planning your heist, improving it, and watching it be successful. This can range from making holes in buildings, using your environment, using vehicles, planks, cables, etc. You can be as creative as you want, every level doesn't have one sole solution and can be completed in essentially infinite ways. It was fun exploring the maps and creating the best routes.

Of course, there are also a decent chunk of levels without any time constraints, but have different quirks to make it challenging. Without spoiling anything, the missions later on get a lot more...interesting. Also, as you beat more missions, you will unlock more tools that will make your life a LOT easier. 

There are also various settings that make the campaign easier, such as adding more time to the alarms or giving you more ammo. You can also use overpowered mods from the workshop in the campaign if you so wish.

All in all,
The story is good.
The maps and levels are high-effort and detailed.
The OST is amazing.
The DLCs I can't comment on as I don't own them, but they seem overpriced to me.

So, if you are looking for a game to just destroy stuff, Teardown is a fine choice.
If you want a puzzle/heist game, play the campaign.
If you want both, then you get the best of both worlds.

Overall, a 10/10 game.

I want to highlight the unique mechanics of the campaign. This consists of three phases: planning, destruction, parkour. The wonderful interplay of these three aspects seems to me to be a bit underrepresented in the reviews I've seen so far. 

The planning phase includes the inspection of all target objects, the existing paths and vehicles. Using the real-time updated bird's eye view, a plan is then made as to how all the goals can be reached as quickly as possible. In most levels, interaction with one of the targets triggers an alarm, which gives you 60 seconds to complete all other level targets. The destructibility of everything is above all the basic condition to be able to create direct paths between the goals. In this way, breathtaking parkour routes are created! If you are aiming to achieve all of the bonus goals, the planning and destruction phase can sometimes take an hour or two. Example: I once spent a very long time bringing down greater parts of a house, only to finally be able to drop parts of the roof onto a well-placed vehicle so that it became a kind of mobile bridge that I could use somewhere else. At some point you either run out of destructive resources or you lose patience and finally want to know if you can do it already. Then the anticipation reaches its maximum and you trigger the countdown through a carefully considered first interaction with one of the targets. This is where the parkour and adrenaline phase begins. Depending on the difficulty of the level, the resources you used and experience you gathered, you can make it or not. If not, you have to try it again. Often your work in the preceding phases just wasn't enough and you have to make further adjustments of the parkour. The  combination of repetition, small adjustments and creative solutions to reach all goals in an even shorter time is very reminiscent of the optimisation process in some speed running. Of course it's less grindy and more catchy and fun. 

I managed to get almost all of the bonus targets in about 30 hours of playing. Even though this is still in beta and the developers have promised that there will be a continuation of the campaign, I would like them to increase the difficulty of the first part of the campaign a little. For example, by introducing a few additional targets or enemies to guard those targets. In general i really like the concept of bonus targets in this game.

I would also really like if the story would be a little less linear. For example: different paths of missions depending on how a level was completed. Or a secret path of missions that is unlocked by completing a level in an unwanted or unconventional manner. 
 
This game is a unique experience and extremely entertaining. It's worth its money, even in beta.

Full destruction, what more is there to say? Well, a lot:

The story is brilliant, how it is told and how it ties the missions together and makes you care, it is all very well done. I can't wait for part two. There is so much potential.

The mission structure is very elegant, no hand holding and lets you figure it out with trial and error(quicksave/load is your friend). You determine how difficult you want it to be by trying to do it all or just the required elements. Long periods of mission prep come with a huge payoff when you make it out of there without getting caught. While there is some repetition in strict terms (steal a bunch of things or break a bunch of things) the variety imparted in each mission keeps it fresh, and the story keeps you motivated. 

The player is rewarded for just poking around each map, there are "valuable items" hidden (sometimes VERY well) around the maps that turn into money you can use to upgrade your kit.  It rewards people like me who like to spend time looking around.

Vehicles: I think the cars are well implemented, some of the construction vehicles (particularly the bulldozer) are a little too fragile to be tremendously useful sometimes.  Boat handling is realistic enough for me. 

I haven't had this much fun with a new game in a long time. There are so many different directions the developers could go with new maps and challenges. I could see an awesome prison break style level or a time limited teardown challenge.

In summary, It's great! The devs really made this into a proper game instead of a tech demo and I'm glad they did so before letting it out into the world. I am eagerly awaiting updates.

The most exhilarating destruction game I've ever experienced - not just by a little bit, by a country mile. Teardown is a top-tier, elite physics game that intertwines problem solving and brute force. The maps are well designed, the assortment of tools and vehicles available are very creative, the engine and voxel environment is sensational. Everything is well executed and performs smoothly - no issues, no crashes, no complaints whatsoever.

It is so fun. I had wrongly assumed this was (just) a sandbox experience but what has really impressed me right from the beginning is the campaign mode. I won't spoil anything for you, but you'll be tasked with assignments of mixed legitimacy that involve looting, heist planning and item acquiring. It does this in a way that keeps you entertained, immersed & constantly wanting to do 'just one more mission'. 

My perception of working against a time limit in games is often negative, but this is what makes the missions on Teardown magic. Having to craft your own route through a map, to collect 5 or 6 different objects, within the space of 60 seconds? It gives the perfect reason to destroy everything that stands in your path of completion. It is a very clever game. The numerous times I've been less than a second away from completing a mission and I've had to go back to the drawing board on what to finesse!

Along with the campaign you get a stellar sandbox experience, steam workshop connected to thousands of mods to test and trial, and even the first DLC campaign absolutely free. And challenges. Steam workshop is wonderful - not only is their a tonne of guns to use but people have spent time creating brilliant maps. Within a few minutes of perusing and downloading from the store, I found myself being chased by a T-Rex & King Kong through the streets of New York. Next I was inside an AT-AT and staring at the Millenium Falcon on a SW inspired map. 

An absolute no brainer from me and one that I'll keep installed for a long, long time. Couldn't recommend it any higher. Get it.

PS. The achievements are great fun and another added component to complete once you finish the campaign.

With this game now launching in 1.0, I have to give it the due respect it deserves and give it a big thumbs up.

When this game was first shown, I just thought "looks like a cool tech demo, but that is all".
When it was then released in early access, I thought "this is a seriously impressive piece of software, but I do not see it becoming an interesting game".

Now in it's current state, I will happily admit that I was completely wrong. The destruction is so satisfying, and all you wish for is more and more. During the campaign you often spend a large amount of time trying to plan stuff out, destroying things in a particular way, setting up planks and vehicles creatively such that you can get all the objectives done in time. When you then complete the level, it is super satisfying. Furthermore the campaign itself is also pretty interesting, with different types of level objectives available, with a nice background story to it all as well. The progression feels great too, with more tools of destruction becoming available to you over time.

My utmost respect to the creators of Teardown. Not only is it an amazing piece of software, it is also a fantastically designed game. I hope to see much more of this engine in the future, and with 1.0 I am really glad to see that the campaign has been extended as well, so that is already a good sign.

STUNNING!!!! A new all-time favorite in the making. 

Simply demolishing your surroundings in sandbox mode would've been more than enough to hold me over, but the game's campaign goes above and beyond being a glorified tutorial or afterthought, and winds up being an absolute FEAT! Not since PORTAL 2 have I had this much fun solving puzzles; not since PHANTOM PAIN has the planning, execution, and getaway felt as liberating; and not since... ever...? has destruction in video games come close to the likes of TEARDOWN.

The open-ended nature of these puzzle box/heist/race-against-the-clock hybrid missions are a brilliant showcase of the game's physics engine where you're constantly met with these small interactions between you and the environment that feel like huge, gratifying "a-ha!" moments. I KNEW destroying things was going to be fun and look amazing but, in the context of these thought-out missions, it feels even more substantial than anticipated. I came into this game ready to crash a yacht into a beach house (and I did just that) but, today, found myself completely enamored by a mission that required me to dispose of 6 heavy safes, scattered across the map, all into the ocean, but — BUT! they were all rigged with an alarm system triggered by exposure to water, AND it was RAINING. So the second I moved any of them out into the open, my 60 second countdown would begin. What I ended up doing was driving various trucks from around the map to each safe and, one at a time, I loaded 'em up. I secured them in place with wooden planks so they wouldn't slide off and I made sure to cover them using large pieces of debris I cut out myself so they wouldn't sound the alarm when I drove off into the rain with them. Only then was I able to usher all of these vehicles to a cliff-side, drive the safes into the water one-by-one, completing my objective AND escaping within 10 SECONDS after just under 2 HOURS of testing and preparation.

The game is packed with moments like this, big and small, and it only opens up more as you play around in it. If you have a crazy idea or potential solution, try it out! Limitations are few and far between so, more often than not, what you want to do is actually doable. Manipulating the destructible environments in your favor as you carefully plot out those 60 seconds are some of the most fun, rewarding, and creatively stimulating moments I've had in a video game, period. And I don't think it's going to be easy for something else to replicate it because of how outstandingly designed Tuxedo Lab's from-the-ground-up foundation is, and not to mention, how good it feels to tear it all down.

As of right now, I cannot recommend the game due to a security risk.

The developers recently added "featured mods" which downloads a ZIP file from their server, which contains XML and image files.

This would be fine, if the developers were using HTTPS for communication, but at this point they are refusing to do that, due to it being "too complicated and requiring too many libraries".

This is 2022, it is unacceptable to use HTTP for a public facing service that downloads content to a user's machine. It leaves the door open for man in the middle attacks (MITM)

They proposed doing zip signing instead, but that will not do any good should a MITM attack occur resulting in a malicious file being downloaded (recall that there were exploits in the past that only required you to download a file, not interact with it, but simply download it, and the exploit relied on a vulnerability in the way Windows Explorer handled icons.) Even if signing was used, all it takes is a vulnerability to occur in the signing verification or even the extraction of the ZIP file (or perhaps one in the XML/image rendering library the game uses) to pwn your machine.

Should all this change and they actually switch to using HTTPS, then I will remove this review, but in the meantime, if you do want to play the game, do so at your own risk, you'll likely be fine, but the risk is always there.

Edit 2022-12-16: 
The domain they use for promos still doesn't support HTTPS.

Edit 2023-11-10:
So I wanna address a few things because some of the folks commenting here seem to be misunderstanding.

Loading the game up, without ANY user interaction AT ALL, before the user even gets to the main menu, a call to the following URL is made

hxxp : // promo.teardowngame . com/promo . php?version=<version number here> (commented out the replaced "tt" with "xx" so that no one accidentally clicks it)

What gets returned is a link to a ZIP file in plain text that the game then automatically downloads and extracts.

In this case it was hxxp : // promo.teardowngame . com/2023-11-01 . zip (again replaced "tt" with "xx" so no one clicks it)

Without ANY interaction at all, without even downloading a mod, simply just launching the game, it makes an unencrypted (thus interceptable on unsecured networks, such as public WiFi networks, and let's not forget that because of things like laptops, and steam decks and whatnot, that the possibility of this is greater than 0%, because it's not unlikely that someone might decide to go to a coffee shop or something with their gaming device and play a bit of gaming while they wait for their order or whatnot) request through HTTP (and I have confirmed this with Wireshark).

All it takes is someone intercepting that request and sending a spoofed response with a different URL, or hell even running a rogue network that points the promo domain to a different server to send back a malicious zip file (and this is possible because with http the client doesn't need to validate the server that is responding because it's unencrypted).

Once again, YOU LITERALLY DO NOT EVEN HAVE TO INTERACT WITH MODS/THE FEATURED MODS BUTTON ON THE MENU OR DO ANYTHING AT ALL BESIDES LAUNCH THE GAME.

If you don't believe me, open up windows explorer, navigate to "%localappdata%\Teardown", look for "promo.txt" and a folder called "promo", delete both of them, and then launch the game but don't do anything, and then look at the folder again. You'll see that it will have recreated the folder and file you just deleted, without you ever doing anything to prompt it to redownload other than just launching the game.

Hell if you open up promo.txt you'll see the URL, and you'll see it is still using HTTP.

I can understand how some people might think it's not a big deal, but when a game gives you no control over disabling it from phoning home (because that's what it is doing, it's connecting to a server that is controlled by the developers to get information about featured mods) and it's not even doing that over an encrypted connection, it's a ticking time bomb just waiting for someone to get hacked.

It doesn't matter if the developers hand pick the mods themselves they feature, that it isn't the problem, the problem is the request is not secure and you'll never truly know if the response you got back, was truly from the server owned by the developers, or a malicious third party who did a MITM (Man-In-The-Middle) attack on your connection.

And yes, they still aren't using HTTPS

It's also comedic, do you know why? 

I got curious about how the featured mod system works, so I took a deeper look at it, the way it works is it uses an XML file to contain the list of featured mods.

For example:

[code]
<item id="steam-3494717963" title="Vox Remover (Performance Mod)" shorttitle="Vox Remover" author="Okidoki" tags="tool" image="tool/voxremover.jpg">
			Remove unwanted shapes, vehicles or clutter with a click. Great for improving performance or cleaning up maps to make space for your own creations.
		</item>
[/code]

The text in between the item tags is the description, the title is the title attribute, short title, author and so on.

The interesting thing is the id attribute, if you modify the the numeric part of the ID, you can change it to any valid teardown workshop ID and it will install it as soon as you hit the "subscribe" button, no validating that the description and title actually match because the developers assume that it would never be tampered with.

This means that instead of getting the mod you think you were getting, you could get an entirely different one if the download of the featured mods zip was intercepted in a Man-In-The-Middle attack, forget doing something like a buffer overflow or anything like that, just being able to trick the user into downloading a mod that isn't the one they thought they were getting is concerning enough, combine that with a malicious lua (the scripting language) script (yes I know there's probably a lua sandbox, but sandbox escapes aren't impossible) and you've essentially have a means of running remote code on an unsuspecting person's system.

Imagine a scenario where you have a group of people together IRL playing Teardown at something like a LAN party, now imagine a bad actor intercepting the DNS requests and pointing the promo domain towards a locally hosted server that serves up a tampered with promos list that is a clone of the real one but with modified IDs, and the new IDs point to recently uploaded workshop files that are hiding malicious lua scripts that once enabled and loaded into a map, could be using a sandbox escape to then run any sort of malware on the victims's systems, anything from stealing credentials to something extreme like ransomware. Seems unlikely sure, but not impossible (I mean you saw the malware incident with Beamng mods and they use lua as well).

Also, the image allows path traversal: "../../../../Pictures/lmao.png" was able to be loaded from my user's pictures directory (not useful, but interesting none the less) doesn't seem to allow loading URLs, but using a hex editor, I kept the image header and stuff to make the mimetype and metadata parsing seems like it's an image, and then replaced the rest of the bytes from an exe file, and attempted to load the featured mods menu and it crashed the game, so I suspect there's possibility of code execution with a tampered image (and well with the path traversal being possible, combine with bad mod and boom, malware executed)

[h1]When all you have is a hammer…[/h1]
[b][i]Teardown[/i][/b] is a voxel-based, first-person puzzle and platformer game centered around destruction. Said destruction is the means by which the player accomplishes daring heists throughout its campaign – and can indulge in freely via the sandbox mode.

Despite the world being made out of tiny blocks, environmental design and art is nothing short of beautiful. Soft post-processing depth of field and motion blur come together to give an authentic, toy-like aesthetic to the levels. This is, of course, helped by the hardware-agnostic raytracing introduced in this title. One doesn’t require a beefy, hyper-expensive RTX or RX graphics card to enjoy the dynamic illumination provided (though they certainly help). Though I must say, the lighting is a little subdued with the lack of prominent bounces and its very soft shadows. I wager it’s instead the fire and particle technologies that truly steal the show – setting buildings on fire, for instance, makes for jaw-dropping displays of dynamic smoke as the hot gasses spread off walls and ceilings, and shoot out from any openings.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2831855969
This cutting-edge technology (as of 2022, anyway) doesn’t come without compromises. On my [i]Ryzen 9 3900X, 32GB RAM, 1070 Ti, Windows 10 Pro[/i] system, running at 1440p 60hz, the highest rendering quality and scaling settings don’t allow for a constant 60fps. While most discrete individual options aren’t available, turning down the rendering quality or especially scaling helps immensely with performance. The softness and fuzziness of 75% scaling (effectively 1080p for me) weren’t intrusive, personally. I also report no major instability or technical issues… however, demolishing half of the map in sandbox mode effectively can cull your framerate to below 30fps, and only a map (or save) reload can help.

And the presentation is finalized by the exquisite soundscape. Level ambience is provided by a varied collection of guitars and percussion, which fit just as well in a spy show. Special consideration must be given to the hectic tune that plays when the alarm goes off. At the same time, crunchy and surprisingly varied sound effects bliss your ears, as the cacophony of destruction ensures you can distinguish concrete, wood and metal from each other right after the potent explosions fade into echoes. Simply smacking your sledgehammer into concrete sounds powerful.
[h3]“I have a slight problem with an old building… and I’d need someone to knock it over.”[/h3]
So, to what end could the player make use of destructible environments? Our featureless protagonist’s business is running into serious debt, prompting them to take up shady jobs from shady individuals. Sure enough, one thing leads to another, and the player is entangled in revenge plots, insurance frauds, and a forensic investigation taking them all across the fictional lands of Löckelle. It’s a wholly ridiculous premise, and rather hilarious at that – almost no one suspects you to be the cause behind absolutely everything being stolen or trashed.

Being mobile is extremely important in a game about heists. Luckily. movement is very forgiving, if rather floaty, in Teardown. The player can squeeze through tiny gaps in the environment, and boasts impressive traversal prowess bordering on parkour. You can’t quite jump onto things higher than your viewpoint, nor can you tether and balance on just one voxel-wide edges – but that’s no problem, since your tools can shape (read: wreck) levels into a more traversable form.

For the majority of the game, heists are what you do. Each heist starts you with a planning phase, in which you’re free to go wherever you want, and to destroy as much as either your heart allows, or your ammunition pools permit. With regards to the destruction itself, it’s rather disappointing that buildings don’t collapse under their own weight. Thin beams of weak wood or even glass can hold entire houses up until that one section is destroyed, at which point the upper floors just fall with minimum spectacle onto the already existing rubble. Tensile strength isn’t simulated, which means there’s predictability in the destruction in most cases, but the actual demolition aspect is significantly downplayed (unless you liberally use explosives to send massive chunks flying out of something).
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2831889856
And yet, blowing everything up isn’t exactly the goal either, at least in the campaign. You instead scope the place out, reposition key objectives as best as you can under the active security systems, set up vehicles as transportation or simple destruction tools, and otherwise cause just enough destruction to speed up your movement between the targets. You do all this because a 60 second timer counts down to failure once the first objective is stolen or triggered. In this sense, you’re playing a puzzle-platformer with an emphasis on speedrunning, which is actually an area where the game is strongest. 

Definitely not the vehicles, though. They get stuck on almost any uneven terrain, including their own fallen body parts, and are otherwise tough to control at high speed. Be cautious around them.

The first half of the campaign is largely composed of timed missions, with occasional breather levels where you simply tear down (ha) some structure or otherwise do a relatively simple task. In the story’s second half, a lot more variation is brought to the table, not all of which sticks the landing in my opinion. Being chased by an attack helicopter is great fun, as you improvise escape routes and try to sneak out of sight, but others are more of a chore to go through; the stakes are lower in many of these, as you just drag heavy objects about with little to stop you.

By completing missions, you rise up the in-game rankings and unlock more tools – securing optional objectives speed up this process. Missions take place in discrete locations which are revisited multiple times over the story, and which also contain hidden items that can be stolen in exchange for money. With said funds, you can improve your tools: more capacity, stronger explosives, better gun range… Your shotgun will be your trusty workhorse for most of the game, especially when fully upgraded – closely followed by placed explosives and planks. I found the standard difficulty to be challenging but manageable; struggling players can increase factors like the time limit and available ammo, while experts can tweak the other way and reduce them.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2831796304
A single playthrough of the campaign on minimum objectives is good for some 15 hours of playtime. Fully cleaning each mission will take a lot longer. Outside of the story, players can test their skills on generic challenges to either collect as much loot before time is up, secure objectives while hounded by a helicopter, or blow up as much of the map as possible. Then there’s the sandbox mode: no pressure, no limitations (except your framerate, eventually), just you and a whole playground to wreck. Lastly, an honourable mention goes to the modding capability, as the Workshop and even built-in mods can provide potentially endless hours of fun.
[h3]…everything looks like a nail.[/h3]
[i]Destruction sandbox and extraordinary graphics showcase - [b]Teardown[/b] shows wavering focus sometimes, but the thrill of the perfect heist and the catharsis of demolition never fade.[/i]

Wall in the way?
Sledgehammer.

Teardown is an immersive sim in disguise, at least in its campaign. There are truly a near infinite number of ways to approach each of the missions and discovering the right one for you and executing a perfect heist is a feeling like no other.

I must say, the core objectives required for progression are very easy so far but completing all the secondary objectives can be unimaginably difficult and will test your planning and execution skills to their fullest limit. I've spent over an hour on some levels trying to collect all the bonus objectives.

I commend Tuxedo Labs for coming up an incredibly unique and puzzling game that I'll be playing for a long time.

Man, I love this game. Mostly because it's so blatantly obvious the developers love this game. It's (possibly ironically since it is a voxel game) the details.. Everything looks and acts as if somebody spent hours on "their baby", perfecting it. 
An example would be that you do multiple jobs in all locations, but those locations have subtle changes on each successive visit. Those changes tell a story and make the world feel so lived-in and alive. 

The corn that was growing in the cornfield next to your scrapyard is harvested and put in crates next time you pass through, the vehicles standing where the farmer left them for the night. 

The race track you visited previously had construction going on and now the helipad is completed and a vehicle, delivered by helicopter, still stands attached to the lifting array, waiting to be moved. 

Things like that. 

As per the game play. There are a good variety of missions that always has some twist to them and mostly the difficulty increases or decreases depending on how devious and/or creative you are. 
There is just something utterly satisfying about spending an hour on ironing out details, just so you can beat a 60 second alarm.
This game is very fun and engaging, but that will soon fall as saber interactive continues to ruin the game.

I've only played this game for roughly four hours, and it has already completely shattered my preconceived notion of what "fully destructible" levels in games should be like. For that alone, I think this game is well worth the price.

Aside from being a very impressive game from a technical standpoint, Teardown is a great game with how it allows you to use your creativity while also presenting you with difficult challenges to overcome, while keeping itself fresh with switching up these challenges throughout the game. The physics are very realistic (except for when a building can somehow still stand because it is connected to the ground by 5 voxels), and the tools given to you are very fun to use. The story keeps itself interesting even though it never gets that deep. Get this game!

A Lego dream come to life — a physics sandbox dressed up as a heist game. It’s less about action, more about clever puzzles: figuring out how to tear the world apart just the right way, shaving seconds off an escape route. Every map feels like a quiet challenge to think smarter, not faster. The destruction is satisfying, but it’s the planning that really sticks. Bought it for the puzzles, stayed for the simple joy of breaking things.

Teardown started off as an incredible indie game, full of creativity and charm. The destructible environments and freedom to experiment made it a standout in the genre. But now, with the introduction of a season pass, it feels like the developers have completely lost sight of what made this game great.

What was once a unique and refreshing experience has been tarnished by the same tired monetization tactics we're used to seeing in big-budget titles. A season pass for an indie game like this? It's unnecessary and honestly feels like a blatant cash grab. The focus has shifted from delivering a fun, engaging experience to squeezing money out of players.

Teardown has lost its magic and charm, and it's sad to see a once great indie game fall into the same trap as the bigger studios. It just isn't the same anymore.

An incredibly entertaining game that combines speed-running, heists, simple physics and puzzle mechanics. 

Pros:

1) Almost everything within each sandbox is destructible, meaning that you can get as creative as you'd like with the way you plan on going about each mission.

2) The story is simple but hilarious and filled with ridiculous amounts of domestic destruction.

3) There's a great amount of replayability value here for those interested since there isn't just one way to succeed in each mission.

4) The aesthetic is both functional toward the nature of the game and visually pleasing.

Cons:

1) The game is quite resource heavy. I would not recommend picking it up if you do not have at least an above-average computer.

2) The physics in the game can bug out at times leading to frustrating re-loads being necessary every once in a while.

3) The ground clearance on vehicles doesn't make too much sense and vehicles get stuck on top of rubble a little too easily.
